headline: Australia's oldest department store calls in experts

sources.title: Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years (BBC)
David Jones goes into administration, with store closures expected and thousands of jobs at risk (The Guardian)
David Jones calls in administrators, leaving retailer's future in doubt (ABC News)

chunks.text: The David Jones company has sold goods in Australia for 188 years. It is the country's oldest [[department store]] chain. Queen Elizabeth attended a [[banquet]] at its Sydney store in 1954. Many Australians {{grew up}} with its Christmas [[window displays]], and some people traveled for hours to see them. On November 5, 2026, the chain's leaders {{called in}} [[administrators]]. These are outside experts who try to save or sell a company in trouble.

verbs.correct: To change from a child to an adult
verbs.wrong: To feel sad about an old memory
verbs.why: Many kids grow up with a dog in the house. Children who grow up near the ocean often swim well. Many Australians grew up with the Christmas window displays at David Jones.

verbs.correct: To ask experts to come and help
verbs.wrong: To pay workers before they leave
verbs.why: Schools call in a plumber when the pipes leak. Companies call in a lawyer when a contract looks wrong. The leaders of David Jones called in administrators on November 5, 2026.

chunks.text: The chain is not closed. Its 38 stores and its website remain open. But many customers have left [[traditional stores]] for online shopping. [[Steep losses]] have {{piled up}} for years. The chain also {{fell behind}} on its rent. Talks with its main [[landlord]], the owner of many [[shopping malls]], {{broke down}}. The landlord said it made a [[generous offer]] to keep the chain open. The owners, an [[investment company]], {{turned down}} the offer.

verbs.correct: To keep growing until it is large
verbs.wrong: To be counted twice by mistake
verbs.why: Bills pile up when people lose their jobs. Debts pile up fast on a credit card. Steep losses have piled up at David Jones for years.

verbs.correct: To be late paying money you owe
verbs.wrong: To pay more than the agreed amount
verbs.why: Many families fall behind on their bills after a job loss. Students sometimes fall behind on their loan payments. David Jones fell behind on its rent.

verbs.correct: To fail because people cannot agree
verbs.wrong: To become loud and very angry
verbs.why: Talks often break down when neither side gives anything. Peace talks break down when trust is low. Talks between the chain and its main landlord broke down.

verbs.correct: To say no to an offer
verbs.wrong: To read a contract with care
verbs.why: Some people turn down a job because the pay is low. Small companies sometimes turn down big offers. The landlord said the chain's owners turned down its offer.

chunks.text: The chain's main [[lender]], the company that lent it money, then chose a second team of experts, called [[receivers]], to protect its loans. That team has {{taken over}} daily control of the business. The owners could not {{turn the business around}}. The administrators are trying to find a buyer. A new buyer could {{step in}}. Business experts expect [[store closures]], mostly in malls far from city centers. The chain has about 6,000 workers, and thousands could be {{laid off}}.

verbs.correct: To get control of a business
verbs.wrong: To give money to a business
verbs.why: Big companies often take over small ones. A son sometimes takes over his father's store. A team of receivers has taken over daily control of David Jones.

verbs.correct: To make a failing business do well
verbs.wrong: To move a business to a new city
verbs.why: A good manager can turn around a failing restaurant. New owners sometimes turn a weak company around. The owners could not turn David Jones around.

verbs.wrong: To let another person take your place
verbs.why: Governments often step in when a big bank is in trouble. Neighbors step in when a family needs help. A new buyer could step in and try to save David Jones.

verbs.correct: To end workers' jobs to save money
verbs.wrong: To move workers to a new store
verbs.why: Factories lay off workers when orders fall. Companies often lay off staff in hard times. Thousands of David Jones workers could be laid off.

chunks.text: The union for [[retail workers]] wants to {{hold on to}} as many jobs as possible. Its leader said a smaller David Jones is better than seeing the chain {{go under}}. An expert at a consumer website told shoppers to {{use up}} their [[gift cards]] quickly. He said the cards will almost certainly be [[worthless]] if no buyer is found. A retail expert at an Australian university said the chain must {{bring back}} good [[customer service]].

verbs.correct: To keep something you could lose
verbs.why: Good bosses try to hold on to their best workers. Families try to hold on to their homes when money is short. The union wants to hold on to as many jobs as possible.

verbs.correct: To fail and stop doing business
verbs.wrong: To move the main office abroad
verbs.why: Many small restaurants go under in their first year. Stores go under when customers stop coming. The union's leader does not want to see David Jones go under.

verbs.wrong: To sell something to a friend
verbs.why: Many people use up their vacation days in December. Families use up their savings when prices rise fast. An expert at a consumer website told shoppers to use up their David Jones gift cards quickly.

verbs.wrong: To ask customers to pay more
verbs.why: Some restaurants bring back old favorites every winter. Some towns bring back old street fairs. A retail expert said David Jones must bring back good customer service.

vocab.def: To keep growing until it is large

vocab.def: To be late paying money you owe

vocab.def: To fail because people cannot agree

vocab.def: To say no to an offer

Her sister took over the family restaurant.

A local bank stepped in with a loan.
Her uncle stepped in when the family needed money.

The company laid off half of its office staff.

vocab.def: To keep something you could lose

ex: The bakery went under after two bad years.
Their airline went under in 2019.

We used up all our vacation days by June.
He used up his phone data in a week.
Use up your coupons before they expire.
The coffee shop brought back its old menu.
The school wants to bring back music classes.
The city brought back its summer concerts after ten years.

wordDefs.def: A large store that sells clothes, home goods and many other things
ex: We bought a new coat at the department store.
The department store has a toy section on the fourth floor.
My aunt worked at a department store for twenty years.

wordDefs.def: A large formal dinner for many people
ex: The school held a banquet for its best athletes.
The mayor gave a short speech at the banquet.
The hotel can serve a banquet for 300 guests.

wordDefs.def: Goods arranged in store windows so people on the street can see them
ex: The shoe store changes its window displays every month.
We walked downtown to look at the window displays.
Bright window displays bring more people into a store.

wordDefs.def: Outside experts who try to save or sell a company in trouble
ex: The court named two administrators to run the failing airline.
The administrators found a buyer for the old factory.
Workers met the administrators to ask about their pay.

wordDefs.def: Real stores in buildings that people visit, not websites
ex: Some people still prefer traditional stores to websites.
Traditional stores let you try clothes on before you pay.
Many traditional stores also sell their goods online.

wordDefs.def: Very large amounts of money that a business loses
ex: The airline reported steep losses after fuel prices rose.
Steep losses forced the company to sell two factories.
Investors worry about steep losses at the car maker.

wordDefs.def: A person or company that owns a place and rents it to others
ex: Our landlord raised the rent by 50 dollars.
Call the landlord if the heat stops working.
My landlord lives on the first floor of the building.

wordDefs.def: Large buildings with many stores inside
ex: Teenagers often meet friends at shopping malls.
Many shopping malls in our state are half empty.
Shopping malls get very busy before Christmas.

wordDefs.def: An offer that gives more than people expect
ex: The company made him a generous offer to stay.
They received a generous offer for their old house.
It was a generous offer, so she said yes right away.

wordDefs.def: A company that buys businesses or other things to make money
ex: An investment company bought the old hotel downtown.
She works for an investment company in Boston.
The investment company sold the farm for a big profit.

wordDefs.def: A bank or company that lends money
ex: Our lender wants the first payment in March.
Compare the rates of more than one lender before you borrow.
The lender agreed to give the farmer more time.

wordDefs.def: Experts chosen by a lender to run a company in trouble
ex: The bank chose receivers to run the failing hotel.
The receivers sold two of the factories in June.
Workers asked the receivers about their missing pay.

wordDefs.def: When a company closes stores and does not open them again
ex: The grocery chain announced ten store closures in Texas.
Store closures left many downtown buildings empty.
Low sales led to store closures across the region.

wordDefs.def: People whose job is to sell goods in stores
ex: Retail workers are very busy in December.
Many retail workers stand all day.
The new law gives retail workers more notice of their schedules.

wordDefs.def: Cards with money on them to spend at a certain store
ex: I gave my nephew two gift cards for his birthday.
Many people buy gift cards in December.
Some gift cards can only be used online.
These old coins are worthless.
A check from a closed account is worthless.
The stock became worthless when the company failed.

wordDefs.def: The help a company gives to people who buy from it
ex: I called customer service about my broken phone.
That hotel is known for its great customer service.
Good customer service keeps people coming to a store.

mainIdea.s: Australia's oldest department store has called in outside experts after years of losses and unpaid rent. Its doors remain open for now, but closures are expected and thousands of jobs are at risk.
mainIdea.why: Losses piled up and the chain fell behind on its rent, so its leaders called in administrators. Stores are open, but thousands of workers could be laid off.

mainIdea.s: A famous Australian retailer asked for help after its landlord suddenly raised the rent. The owners accepted a rescue deal from the landlord, but experts still expect some stores to close.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the problem was not a sudden rent increase. The chain fell behind on its rent, and the landlord said the owners turned its offer down.

mainIdea.s: David Jones will open a large new location in Sydney to mark 188 years in business. The company plans to hire more staff next year and create bigger Christmas windows for visiting families.
mainIdea.why: Nothing new is opening. David Jones called in administrators, and a team of receivers has taken over daily control of the business.

tf.s: David Jones called in outside experts after years of heavy losses.
tf.why: Steep losses piled up for years. On November 5, 2026, the chain's leaders called in administrators, who try to save or sell a company in trouble.

tf.s: The chain has closed all of its stores and its website.
tf.why: The stores and the website remain open, even though receivers have taken over daily control of the business.

tf.s: David Jones fell behind on the rent it owed its main landlord.
tf.why: The chain fell behind on its rent, and talks with the owner of many shopping malls broke down.

tf.s: The landlord turned down a rescue offer from the chain's owners.
tf.why: It was the other way. The landlord said it made a generous offer, and the chain's owners turned it down.

tf.s: Thousands of David Jones workers could be laid off.
tf.why: The chain has about 6,000 workers. Business experts expect store closures, and the union wants to hold on to as many jobs as possible.

tf.s: An expert at a consumer website told shoppers to save gift cards for later.
tf.why: He told shoppers to use up their gift cards quickly. He said the cards will almost certainly be worthless if no buyer is found.

lines.text: Did you hear about David Jones, the big department store chain in Australia?
Its leaders {{called in}} outside experts. They're trying to save the company or sell it.
Wow. That's [[hard to imagine]]. Is it closed?
No, the stores are open [[for the time being]]. But the chain {{fell behind}} on its rent.
How did it get so bad?
Losses {{piled up}} for years. Then talks with its main landlord {{broke down}}.
Didn't the landlord try to help?
It says it made a generous offer, but the owners {{turned it down}}.
So who's running the stores now?
A second team of experts has {{taken over}}. And thousands of jobs are [[on the line]].
I [[feel bad for]] those workers. Will many get {{laid off}}?
Thousands could. The union wants to {{hold on to}} as many jobs as possible.
One expert says to {{use up}} your gift cards [[while you still can]].
Good advice. Could a new buyer {{step in}}?
Maybe. But that buyer would need to {{turn the business around}}.
A lot of people {{grew up}} with those Christmas windows. I hope it survives.

expressions.def: Used to say that something seems very surprising or unlikely
ex: A town without its old theater is hard to imagine.
It's hard to imagine summer without the beach.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is true now but may change
ex: We're staying with my parents for the time being.
The road is closed for the time being.

expressions.def: Used to say that something could be lost if things go badly
ex: My job is on the line if this project fails.
The team's whole season is on the line tonight.

expressions.def: Used to say that you are sorry about someone's problems
ex: I feel bad for the kids who missed the trip.
We feel bad for our neighbors after the fire.

expressions.def: Used to tell someone to act before the chance is gone
ex: Buy your tickets while you still can.
Enjoy the warm weather while you still can.
